thread.title: Trump Tariffs: Only A Stock Market Rout Can Avert A Trump Trade War

author: JED GRAHAM
title: Trump Tariffs: Only A Stock Market Rout Can Avert A Trump Trade War
text:
The U.S. economy is cruising along so well right now that it might take a stock-market rout to avert a Trump trade war.
X President Donald Trump touts his economic record on pretty much a daily basis of late and feels like he is launching trade conflicts from a position of strength. Now that verbal bombs aimed at Europe, Canada, Mexico, China and others are being followed by live tariffs and retaliatory action, the prospect for talks have never looked so dim.
The trade conflict seems likely to get worse before it gets better. Meanwhile, Republicans in Congress have largely ruled out trying to wrest control of trade policy back from the White House.
The only thing that might stop a trade war in its tracks — before the costs escalate — would be a suddenly lousy stock market that begins to put Trump's economic record and GOP control of Congress in jeopardy.

Will Trump Trade War Bow To The Dow? That's why the stock market, whose current prices adjust to reflect altered expectations for earnings and economic growth over the intermediate term, seems to be the most likely catalyst to head off a widening Trump trade war.
But right now, stock markets appear only slightly worried. On Friday, the Trump administration said that it will impose 25% tariffs on $34 billion worth of mostly high-tech imports from China on July 6. That spurred China to announce $34 billion in retaliatory tariffs. The Dow Jones industrial average and S&P 500 index sold off initially, but rallied to close Friday with modest losses.
After a weak open Monday on the stock market today , the Dow Jones pared losses but notch its fifth straight down session, falling 0.4%. The S&P 500 closed 0.2% lower, and tech-heavy Nasdaq composite ended at break-even levels.
Stock-Market Jekyll And Hyde For now, investors are cautiously optimistic, but that may not hold. Ed Yardeni, chief investment strategist of Yardeni Research, wrote that his bullish stock-market outlook requires Trump's "benevolent Dr. Jekyll persona" of tax-cutter and deregulator to triumph over his protectionist Mr. Hyde.
"If his tariffs trigger widespread retaliation and an outright global trade war, then earnings will take a dive," Yardeni wrote. "We continue to expect that it will all end peaceably. But it isn't heading in that direction right now."
UniCredit Group chief economist Erik Nielsen wrote that he thinks markets are too optimistic about the risk of a broadening trade war and sees potential for "some rough months ahead in global equity markets."
"Markets haven't taken this increasingly serious risk into account, but rather focused on the ongoing macro developments, possibly dismissing Trump's threats," Nielsen wrote.
Trade War Extends Beyond Tariffs Here's something to keep in mind: A couple of months before imposing retaliatory tariffs on the U.S., China suddenly stopped buying soybeans from U.S. farmers , shifting orders to Brazil and Canada. Suddenly, China started subjecting shipments of Ford Motor ( F ) vehicles, apples and pork to closer inspection and other regulatory hurdles .
A Trump trade war can hurt U.S. multinationals with big China exposure like Caterpillar ( CAT ), Boeing ( BA ) and Apple ( AAPL ) beyond official tariffs or quotas. The U.S. increasingly looks as if it is headed into a technological cold war with China. China doesn't want to disrupt its economy as it is still developing its technological capabilities. But Beijing may seek opportunities to steer business to non-U.S. countries as it looks to divide America from potential allies in a trade war vs. China.
After Trump appeared ready to greenlight component sales to ZTE, bringing it back from the dead, China seemed ready to sign off on the Qualcomm ( QCOM ) takeover of NXP Semiconductors. Yet now the Qualcomm deal may again be in jeopardy .
On Monday, Qualcomm stock fell 1.1%. As for notable Dow Jones stocks, Caterpillar and Boeing closed down 0.9%. Apple, which outsources its iPhone manufacturing in China, edged 0.1% lower.
Trump seemed to understand this dynamic when he kicked around the idea of joining the Trans-Pacific Partnership trading bloc. Yet Trump has instead stiff-armed U.S. allies in trade talks and weakened his leverage with China. So it may take a stock-market tumble to convince Trump that the trade-war campaign isn't working.
After the stock market panned his steel and aluminum tariffs , Trump, albeit temporarily, granted broad exemptions that minimized both their economic impact and investor concern.
